text: In 1908, Argentina was one of the ten richest countries on Earth.
Richer than France. Richer than Germany. Richer than Canada.
Today, the average Canadian earns two and a half times as much as the average Argentine.
And here's what makes it so strange.
On paper, these two countries are almost twins.
Both are huge. Both are mostly empty.
Both have some of the best farmland on the planet. The Pampas in the south. The Prairies in the north.
Both filled up with millions of European immigrants, at almost exactly the same time.
Both got rich the same way: grain and beef, shipped across the Atlantic to Britain.
Same land. Same people. Same customers.
So why did one keep climbing, and the other start falling?
The answer isn't in the soil.
It's in who owned it.
To see why, we have to go back to the moment these two countries were born as farming giants. And we have to look at them side by side, the way almost nobody does.
Let's start with the land itself.

Look at the Prairies. A sea of grass, flat to the horizon, sitting on some of the deepest black soil in the world. Cold winters. Short summers. But in those few warm months, the ground explodes with life.
Now look at the Pampas. Another sea of grass, just as flat, with soil just as rich. Milder winters. Longer seasons. Rain that falls almost exactly when crops need it.

Underneath both of them lies the same kind of treasure. Geologists call it mollisol. Dark, crumbly, deep soil, built up over thousands of years by grass roots that grew, died and rotted in place. It is some of the most fertile ground anywhere on Earth.
The two regions even look alike from space. Two great green and gold rectangles of grassland, one in each hemisphere, almost mirror images of each other.
Nature dealt these two countries nearly the same hand.
What they did with it is the whole story.
If you had to bet on one of them in eighteen eighty, you would have bet on the Pampas. It was warmer, closer to the ocean, and it already had a great port city sitting right at its edge.
And for a while, that bet would have looked brilliant.
In eighteen ninety, Argentina was already richer per person than Canada.
The railways came first. British money poured into Argentina and laid thousands of miles of track, fanning out from Buenos Aires across the plains like the spokes of a wheel.
Every new line opened new land. Every new field needed hands.
And the hands came.

Between eighteen eighty and nineteen thirty, around six million Europeans sailed to Argentina. Italians, Spaniards, French, Germans. In some years, almost a third of the people living in Buenos Aires had been born somewhere else.

Buenos Aires turned into one of the great cities of the world. Wide avenues. Palaces. Electric trams. In nineteen eight, the same year our story starts, it opened the Teatro Colón, one of the finest opera houses on the planet.
Five years later, in nineteen thirteen, Buenos Aires opened the first subway line in all of Latin America. Before Madrid. Before Tokyo.
Wealthy Argentine families spent so lavishly in Paris that the French had an expression for someone who was absurdly rich. Rich as an Argentine.

By nineteen fourteen, British companies had built tens of thousands of kilometers of railway across the country. Trains carried grain and cattle from the plains straight to the docks of Buenos Aires and Rosario.
For the people who owned that land, it was a golden age.
Meanwhile, Canada was still almost empty.

The Canadian Pacific Railway reached the Pacific in eighteen eighty five, but for years the trains crossed the Prairies carrying almost nobody. Settlers preferred the United States. The Canadian West was too cold, too far, too unknown.

And that railway was a gamble of its own. To convince British Columbia to join the new country, Canada had promised to connect it to the east by rail. The line had to cross the Canadian Shield, the open Prairies and the Rocky Mountains.
On the seventh of November, eighteen eighty five, in a mountain pass called Craigellachie, a railway executive hammered in the last spike. Canada was finally tied together from ocean to ocean.
Now the country had a railway, and nobody to ride it.
So Canada did something unusual. It started selling the Prairies like a product.
The government printed millions of posters and pamphlets, in a dozen languages. They called the Prairies the Last Best West. Free farms for the millions.
Agents travelled across Britain, Scandinavia, Germany and Eastern Europe with lantern slides and photographs of golden wheat.
The man behind the campaign was Clifford Sifton, Canada's Minister of the Interior. He knew exactly who he wanted. Not city clerks. Farmers. People used to hard winters and hard work.
Years later, he described his ideal settler as a stalwart peasant in a sheepskin coat, born on the soil, with a stout wife and a half dozen children.
It sounds harsh today. But it tells you what Canada was really after. Not workers. Families that would put down roots.

And it worked. Between eighteen ninety six and nineteen fourteen, around three million immigrants came to Canada. Saskatchewan and Alberta went from empty territory to full provinces in less than a decade.
Both countries were now booming the same way.
They grew wheat. They raised cattle. They loaded it onto ships and sent it to Britain, which needed to feed millions of factory workers.
Argentina became one of the biggest exporters of wheat, corn and beef in the world. Canada became one of the biggest exporters of wheat.
Same land. Same people. Same customers.
But underneath that boom, there was one difference. And it was hiding in a piece of paper.
In Canada, that piece of paper was called the Dominion Lands Act.

Before a single settler arrived, the government surveyed the entire Prairie into a giant grid. Townships, six miles by six miles. Each township cut into thirty six sections. Each section cut into four quarters.
One quarter section was a hundred and sixty acres.
And here was the deal. Pay a ten dollar fee. Live on the land for three years. Build a house. Break the ground and farm it.
Do that, and the land was yours. Free.
Not rented. Not borrowed. Yours.
Imagine you are a farmer from Ukraine or Norway in nineteen hundred. You own nothing. And suddenly a government is offering you a farm of your own, bigger than anything your family has ever had.
Hundreds of thousands of families took that deal.

They built sod houses, then wooden houses. They planted wheat. In nineteen nine, a new variety called Marquis wheat ripened faster than the frost, and the Prairies became one of the great breadbaskets of the world.
And because every farmer owned his land, every farmer had a reason to improve it. To drain it, fence it, buy machinery, plant trees, build a better barn.
Towns grew every few miles along the railway. Each one with a grain elevator, a school, a church and a general store. Built by owners, for owners.

Life on a homestead was not romantic. The first house was often made of blocks of sod cut straight from the prairie. Winters could drop to forty below. Families burned straw and dried dung to keep warm, and many gave up and walked away before the three years were over.
But the ones who stayed had something no landlord could take from them. A title deed with their own name on it.

And all along the railway rose tall wooden grain elevators, one in every town. People called them the prairie sentinels. You could see the next town's elevator from miles away, standing alone on the horizon.
But first, there is something important to say about Canada.

The Prairies weren't empty either. Cree, Blackfoot, Assiniboine, Saulteaux and Métis people had lived there for generations. Through a series of treaties, often signed under pressure and broken afterwards, the Canadian government took control of most of that land.
So both countries took the land from the people who were already there. That part of the story is not so different.
The difference is what each country did with the land once it had it.
Now look at Argentina.
In Argentina, the Pampas weren't empty when the boom started. Much of the southern Pampas was still controlled by Indigenous peoples.
In the late eighteen seventies, the government launched a military campaign to take it. History calls it the Conquest of the Desert.
And to pay for that war, the government did something that would shape the country for a century.
It sold the land before it had even conquered it.
Investors bought bonds that could be exchanged for land. When the army pushed the frontier south, those bonds turned into enormous blocks of territory.
Not quarter sections. Estates measured in tens of thousands of acres.
The land went to the people who already had money and connections in Buenos Aires. Ranchers, merchants, politicians. Families whose names you can still find on streets and buildings today.
By the time the immigrants arrived, the best land of the Pampas already belonged to someone.
So what did six million immigrants do in a country where the land was already taken?
They rented.
An Italian family would arrive, sign a contract with an estancia owner, and farm a piece of land for three or four years. Then the contract ended, and they moved on to the next one.
They didn't own the soil. So why would they improve it? Why build a solid house you'll leave in three years? Why plant trees you'll never see grow?
Many immigrants didn't even stay. They came for the harvest and sailed back to Italy every year. People called them golondrinas. Swallows.

And in nineteen twelve, the tenants of Santa Fe finally had enough. Thousands of farmers went on strike against the rents they were paying. It became known as the Grito de Alcorta. The cry of Alcorta.

It started on the twenty fifth of June, in a small town in the south of Santa Fe. Within weeks, the strike had spread across the province. Out of it came the Argentine Agrarian Federation, the first great union of small farmers in the country.
They won lower rents and longer contracts. But they did not win the one thing they really wanted. The land itself.
Same land as the Prairies. Same wheat. Same kind of people.
And here's the strangest part. Argentina actually knew the other way worked.
Back in eighteen fifty six, a group of Swiss, German and French families founded a farming colony called Esperanza, in the province of Santa Fe. Each family received its own plot of land to own.
Esperanza thrived. Dozens of colonies followed. Towns, mills, schools, co-operatives. For a few decades, that corner of Santa Fe looked a lot like the Canadian Prairies.
But the colonies stayed an exception. Out on the great southern Pampas, the land had already been sold in giant blocks.
So one country turned its immigrants into owners. The other turned them into tenants.

The historian Carl Solberg spent years comparing exactly these two regions, the Prairies and the Pampas. And this is the gap he kept coming back to. Not the soil. Not the climate. The rules about who gets to own it.
Why does that matter so much?
Because ownership changes everything that comes after.
An owner borrows against his land to buy a tractor. A tenant can't.
An owner builds a town and pays for a school, because his children will grow up there. A tenant moves on.
An owner votes. And in Canada, a nation of farm owners formed co-operatives, grain pools and even political parties. They pushed back against railways, banks and governments.
In nineteen twenty one, a party called the United Farmers of Alberta won the provincial election and governed the province for fourteen years.
In nineteen twenty four, Prairie farmers created the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, so they could sell their grain together instead of one by one.
And in nineteen thirty two, in Calgary, farmers and workers founded a new party that would later give Canada public health care.
These were not landlords. They were ordinary families with a hundred and sixty acres. And because they owned something, they organized to protect it.

In Argentina, most immigrants never even became citizens. They worked the land, but they had almost no voice in how the country was run. Power stayed with the small group of families who owned the estancias and the capital.

And the ones who complained could be thrown out. In nineteen oh two, Argentina passed the Residence Law, which allowed the government to deport any foreigner it considered a threat to public order. It was used against union leaders and strikers for decades.
In nineteen twelve, Argentina passed a law that made voting secret and compulsory for men. Four years later, voters elected Hipólito Yrigoyen, a president from outside the old elite.
It looked like the country was opening up.
But millions of the people who actually worked the land were foreigners, and foreigners could not vote.
And when a country's wealth and power sit in a few hands, it works fine while the money keeps coming. The trouble starts when it stops.
And in nineteen twenty nine, it stopped.
The Great Depression hit both countries hard. Wheat prices collapsed. In nineteen thirty two, Argentina and Canada were almost exactly as rich as each other again.
But they reacted in completely different ways.
In Canada, the crisis was brutal, but the system held. Governments came and went through elections. Farmers organized. Institutions bent, but they didn't break.
The Prairies were hit by drought, dust storms and grasshoppers. People called it the Dirty Thirties. Thousands of families lost everything.
But they did not lose their country's rules.

In fact, the crisis made the institutions stronger. In nineteen thirty four, Canada created its own central bank, the Bank of Canada. A year later, it set up the Canadian Wheat Board to stabilize the price farmers got for their grain.
The answer to the disaster was more rules, not fewer. And the rules were made by people who had to win elections.
In Argentina, in September of nineteen thirty, the army took power in a coup. It was the first of six military coups in the twentieth century.
The old landowning elite came back to power. In nineteen thirty three, Argentina signed a deal with Britain to protect its beef exports, on terms that many Argentines saw as a humiliation.
The thirteen years that followed have a name in Argentine history. The Infamous Decade. Elections were held, but they were rigged so openly that the politicians in charge called it patriotic fraud.
The cattle barons and the grain exporters were back at the center of the state, and the immigrant farmers were back on the outside.
And from there, the country entered a long cycle. Coups. Populist governments. Inflation. Price controls. Debt. Default. And then, all over again.
Look at what happened next.
By nineteen forty five, Canada was already sixty percent richer than Argentina per person.

In nineteen forty six, Juan Perón was elected president. He promised to take power away from the old landowners and give it to the workers in the cities. He nationalized the British railways, raised wages and built a new kind of state.

For many Argentines, it felt like justice. But it also set off a pattern that would last for decades. Every government tried to undo the last one. Rules changed with every new leader. And when the rules keep changing, nobody wants to invest for the long term.
In nineteen eighty nine, prices in Argentina rose by more than three thousand percent in a single year. A loaf of bread could cost more in the afternoon than it did in the morning.
By nineteen ninety, Canada was almost three times richer.
In nineteen ninety one, Argentina tried a radical cure. It fixed the peso to the US dollar, one to one, by law. Inflation vanished almost overnight, and for a few years the country felt rich again.
But a currency can't be stronger than the country behind it. Debt kept growing. Exports got too expensive. And by the end of the decade, the economy was sinking.
In two thousand one, Argentina defaulted on its debt in what was then the largest sovereign default in history. People lined up outside banks that wouldn't give them their own savings.

In December of that year, the government froze bank accounts to stop people from withdrawing their money. Argentines called it the corralito, the little fence. Within two weeks, the country went through five presidents.
Canada had its own crises. But it never fell off the road.

Remember that party the farmers founded in Calgary? In nineteen forty four, it won power in Saskatchewan, led by a former preacher named Tommy Douglas. In nineteen sixty two, Saskatchewan launched public medical insurance, and within a decade the whole country had followed.
An idea born among wheat farmers with a hundred and sixty acres each ended up shaping the entire nation.

And Argentina's farmland never stopped being rich. Today the country is still one of the biggest food exporters on Earth, and the world's largest exporter of soybean meal. The Pampas still feed millions of people.
The soil never failed Argentina. What failed was the deal that decided who would own it, and who would only work on it.
Now, land is not the only reason. Wars, politics, trade, bad luck and bad decisions all played a part.

Canada had advantages Argentina didn't. It sat right next to the largest economy in the world. It inherited British parliamentary institutions. And through both world wars, it fought alongside Britain and the United States, with guaranteed buyers for everything it could grow.
But none of that explains why two plains, settled at the same time by the same kind of people, produced such different societies on the ground. For that, you have to look at the land.
So think about where it started.

One country handed out a hundred and sixty acres, free, to almost anyone willing to farm it. It built millions of small owners, people with a stake in the country, people with a reason to invest and a voice to defend it.

The other country split the same kind of land into giant estates, owned by a few hundred families, before the immigrants ever arrived. It built a handful of landlords, and millions of people renting the ground under their feet.
Same land. Same people. Same customers.
Different owners.
And more than a century later, you can still see that difference in the numbers.
So here's my question for you. If your country had a Pampas or a Prairie, who owned it? Tell me in the comments. I read every single one.
And if you want to see the next story like this, subscribe. Because next time, we're going to look at two countries that started from exactly the same place, and ended up as opposites.
